notes:
I've written notes for 16 of the 17 verses. I found nothing on v. 12. The Catholic and Orthodox sites and the popular-teaching views (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace) didn't appear in any of my searches, so they're left out. A few things to know before you use these:

- **The tradition labels are mine.** I didn't reach any denominational sites (Ligonier, LCMS, Wesley Center and so on) on this chapter. The disagreements below come from older commentators gathered on Bible Hub and StudyLight. Where I say a writer belongs to a tradition, the pages themselves don't say so; check before you print it.
- **The Precept Austin page was cut off** after its introduction, so I only have its notes on vv. 1, 6 and 16.
- **The Bible Hub "Study Bible" and "What Does … Mean" sections are unsigned.** I've marked them as such.

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1:** The nations are called to stand before the Judge of "the living and the dead" and hear his verdict. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-34-commentary. Guzik says the warning is aimed at the nations, not at God's people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-34/

**v. 2:** Matthew Henry: God has long let the nations go their own way (Acts 14:16). Now that they have all enjoyed his patience, they must expect his anger. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_034.cfm. Henry also says that once God has doomed them, their destruction is as certain as if it had already happened. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_034.cfm

**v. 3:** Coffman links the unburied dead and the blood that melts the mountains to his picture of the final "Great Day." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/34-4.html

**v. 4:**
- **Literal end of the world.** Keil and Delitzsch say the wording is too strong to mean anything other than the end of the world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-4.htm. The Pulpit Commentary sees the actual frame of the heavens dissolving and links it to Matthew 24:29 and 2 Peter 3:10. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/34-4.htm
- **Symbol of human rulers falling.** Barnes reads it as the destruction of princes and nobles who opposed God. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/isaiah/34-4.html. Gill also takes it of the removal of "all dignities and offices," civil and church, within the Roman world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-4.htm
- **How it looks to people.** Calvin compares it to a dark, stormy sky in which the sun and stars seem to faint. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/34-4.html. The Geneva note says the verse speaks as terrified people experience it, as if heaven and earth were perishing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-4.htm
- **Other notes.** Ellicott says no prophetic "day of the Lord" scene was complete without this imagery. It sets the short life of the sun, moon and stars against the eternity of God. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/34-4.htm. Oswalt (quoted on Precept Austin) calls it a reversal of creation: God spread the heavens out like a tent, and now he rolls them back up. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-34-commentary
- **Modern scholarship.** The Cambridge Bible notes Bickell's suggestion that "the host of heaven" is a later scribal addition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-4.htm

**v. 5:**
- **Why Edom.** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Edom gloated over Judah's fall and killed Jews the Babylonians had left behind. God therefore held it guilty of killing a brother, since Esau was Jacob's brother. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-34.html. Guzik treats Edom as one example of the judgment coming on all nations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-34/
- **The sword "bathed in heaven."** Henry thinks this may refer to a custom of soaking swords to harden or polish them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_034.cfm
- **Modern scholarship.** A NET Bible note says Edom stands for all the hostile nations that oppose God. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=isa&chapter=34

**v. 6:**
- **Guzik:** The sacrifice imagery means the judgment is a payment for sin, though "imperfect, incomplete." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-34/
- **Henry:** The whole earth would have been soaked with sinners' blood if Christ had not shed his. Those who reject him become victims of God's wrath themselves. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_034.cfm
- **Wolf (quoted by Guzik):** The sacrificial animals stand mainly for people being slaughtered. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-34/
- **Precept Austin:** It connects Bozrah with Armageddon, noting the two are about 200 miles apart (Revelation 14:20). https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-34-commentary

**v. 7:** The KJV's "unicorns" is better translated "wild oxen." Motyer notes that wild oxen were never sacrificed, so they may stand for Edom's leaders. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-34/

**v. 8:** Keil and Delitzsch call "to contend for Zion" a flash of lightning that lights up the whole prophecy: God takes up Zion's case against its accusers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-10.htm. Henry says Zion has left her cause with God, and he will repay her persecutors at the set time. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_034.cfm

**v. 9:**
- **Sodom imagery.** Utley says pitch and brimstone recall Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24), which lay near Edom. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-34. Constable makes the same link and adds that the chapter stops naming Edom after v. 9. That shows a judgment much wider than one nation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/34-10.html
- **Guzik:** This points to worldwide ecological disaster in the Great Tribulation (Revelation 8, 16). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-34/

**v. 10:**
- **Punishment that fits the crime.** Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note that Edom's first offence was refusing to let Israel pass through. Now no one will pass through Edom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-10.htm
- **Fulfilled in history.** The Pulpit Commentary sees a largely literal fulfilment and cites Malachi 1:3–4. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/34-10.htm. Barnes uses Burckhardt's travels as evidence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-10.htm
- **Calvin:** The ever-burning fire removes any hope of pardon for Edom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/34-10.html
- **Keil and Delitzsch:** The unquenchable fire proves the end of all things is meant. Edom also stands for everyone who behaves like Edom toward God's people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-10.htm
- **Gill:** He reads it as the burning of Rome in Revelation 18–19. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-10.htm
- **Henry:** He applies it to the torment of hell. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/34-10.html
- **Utley:** He calls the language exaggeration for effect, meaning destruction that lasts indefinitely. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-34

**v. 11:** Utley says "chaos" and "emptiness" (tohu and bohu) are the words Genesis 1:2 uses for the world before creation. Edom is sent back to that chaos. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-34. Guzik: in many places only wild animals will be able to live. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-34/

**v. 13 (with vv. 11–15):** Henry applies these verses to the way flourishing cities and lands fall into ruin under God's providence. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_034.cfm

**v. 14:**
- **Guzik:** "Night creature" is *lilith* in Hebrew. The wild goat (KJV "satyr") and Lilith may be ordinary animals, or they may mean demons living in the ruins. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-34/
- **Barnes:** It is a night-spectre from Jewish superstition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-14.htm
- **Clarke:** It is simply a night bird. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/34-14.html
- **Coffman:** The meaning is uncertain, and it might be a demon. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/34-14.html
- **Modern scholarship.** One note on the Bible Hub page traces Lilith to Babylonian demonology. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-14.htm. The NET Bible dictionary calls the evidence a "close balance of probabilities." It also notes that most of the creatures in the list are ordinary animals. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=Night-Monster

**v. 15:** The New Layman's Bible Commentary (quoted by Coffman) says the verse shows that no human beings remain. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/34-10.html

**v. 16:**
- **What "the book of the Lord" is.** The Pulpit Commentary says it is Isaiah's own collected prophecies, since there is no evidence of an earlier collection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-16.htm. Gill mentions Jewish readings that take it as the Law of Moses or Genesis (the animals gathered to Noah in pairs). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/34-16.html. Got Questions also says it means Isaiah's prophecy, as part of Scripture. https://www.gotquestions.org/book-of-the-Lord.html
- **"His Spirit gathers them."** Henry and Poole say the Spirit gathers the animals by instinct, as the animals came to Adam and to Noah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/34-16.html. Ellicott takes "Spirit" as God's creative breath at work in nature (Psalm 104:30). https://biblehub.com/isaiah/34-16.htm
- **Guzik:** Isaiah expects the prophecy to be read "literally – poetically, but literally." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-34/
- **Modern scholarship.** One note on the Bible Hub page argues that "book of Jehovah" assumes a collection of prophetic books already existed, which points to a late date for this chapter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-16.htm

**v. 17:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: as conquerors divide land by lot, God has marked Edom out for the wild animals. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/isaiah-34.html. Henry: Jerusalem rises from its ruins, but the church's enemies stay desolate forever. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_034.cfm

## Where Protestant interpreters differ

**When and how the chapter is fulfilled (whole chapter, especially vv. 1–4 and 10):**
- **Dispensational.** Guzik reads it as the Great Tribulation and Armageddon, with the church escaping beforehand. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-34/. Precept Austin insists it concerns literal Israel. It criticises Ortlund for applying the chapter to "us," which it calls allegorising. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-34-commentary
- **Henry.** He sees layers: first the Assyrians or Nebuchadnezzar, then all enemies of God's kingdom, then the final judgment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_034.cfm
- **Gill.** He reads Edom as Rome. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/34-10.htm

**v. 4, how literal it is:** Pulpit and Keil and Delitzsch take it as the real collapse of the heavens. Calvin and the Geneva note take it as how things will look to frightened people. (Sources under v. 4.)

## Gaps
- Nothing on v. 12.
- Nothing from the Catholic, Orthodox or popular-teaching sources.
